## Continuous Variables (Numerical)

### Statistical Summaries 

The following tables display the summary statistics for the continuous predictor variables. Metrics include mean, median, standard deviation, IQR, Q1, Q3, Minimum, Maximum, and Range. The information regarding each variable are indicated as: 

34. `age`: Patient age ranges from 19 to 96 years old. 
35. `bmi`: Body Mass index is a measure of body fat based on height and weight that applies to adult men and women. The accpetable range of BMI is between 18.5 and 24.9. 
36. `d_dimer_value`:  Measurement of a protein fragment called D-dimer, which is released when blood clots break down. Elevated d-dimer levels are considered to be levels above the thresholds: 500 ng/mL or 0.5 ug/mL. 
37. `bnp_levels`: Measurement of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels in the blood, which is a hormone produced by the heart. Elevated BNP levels are considered to be levels above the threshold: 100 pg/mL. 
38. `echo_rvsp_value`: Measurement of right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) in mmHg. Normal right ventricular systolic pressures are generally considered to be less than 40 mmHg. 
39. `heart_rate`:  A normal resting heart rate for adults ranges from 60 to 100 beats per minute. 
40. `systolic`: Systolic Blood Pressure measures the pressure in the arteries when the heart contracts and pumps blood out. 
41. `diastolic`: Diastolic Blood Pressure measures the pressure in the arteries when the ehart is resting betwen beats.
42. `map_value`: Mean Arterial Pressure is an average pressure in the arteries over a cardiac cycle. Normal MAP values are considered to be greater than or equal to 65 mmHg. Abnormal MAP values are considered to be less than 65 mmHg. 

```{r}
continuous_vars <- c("age", "bmi", "d_dimer_value", "bnp_levels", 
                    "echo_rvsp_value", "heart_rate", "systolic", "diastolic", "map_value")
summarize_continuous <- function(data, var_name) {
  var_data <- data[[var_name]]
  
  summary_stats <- data.frame(
    Mean = round(mean(var_data, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Median = round(median(var_data, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    SD = round(sd(var_data, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    IQR = round(IQR(var_data, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Q1 = round(quantile(var_data, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Q3 = round(quantile(var_data, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Min = round(min(var_data, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Max = round(max(var_data, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Range = round(max(var_data, na.rm = TRUE) - min(var_data, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  )
  
  return(summary_stats)
}

cont_summaries <- list()
for (var in continuous_vars) {
  if (var %in% names(merged_data_no_covid)) {
    cont_summaries[[var]] <- summarize_continuous(merged_data_no_covid, var)
  }
}

master_continuous_summary <- do.call(rbind, cont_summaries)
master_continuous_summary %>%
  kable("html", caption = "Summary Statistics for Continuous Predictor Variables") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
                full_width = FALSE, position = "center")
```


### Visualizations: Box Plots 

The box plots for all the continuous predictor variables are shown below. The potential outliers are highlighted in red. 

```{r}
create_boxplot_trimmed <- function(data, var_name, lower = 0.05, upper = 0.95) {
  values <- data[[var_name]]
  if (is.numeric(values)) {
    q_low <- quantile(values, lower, na.rm = TRUE)
    q_high <- quantile(values, upper, na.rm = TRUE)
    
    ggplot(data, aes(y = !!sym(var_name))) +
      geom_boxplot(fill = "#3498DB", alpha = 0.7, outlier.color = "red") +
      coord_cartesian(ylim = c(q_low, q_high)) +
      labs(
        title = paste("Boxplot of", var_name),
        y = var_name,
        x = NULL
      ) +
      theme_minimal() +
      theme(
        plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold")
      )
  }
}

box_plots <- map(continuous_vars, ~ {
  if (.x %in% names(merged_data_no_covid)) {
```

# Part D: Stratified Analysis (Bivariate): 
**Stratifying individuals by the presence of Pulmonary Embolism: **

In this section, a bivariate analysis is conducted to examine the distribution of predictor variables stratified by the presence (1) or absence (0) of pulmonary embolism (PE). This approach allows for the assessment of potential associations between each predictor and the PE outcome.

## Categorical Variables: Stratified Analysis 

The bivariate analysis first focuses on the **categorical variables**, evaluating differences in their distributions across PE status groups.

### Statistical Summary Table (Cross-Tabulations) 

The table below summarizes a comparison of two patient groups: **Group 1**, consisting of patients diagnosed with pulmonary embolism (PE) (n = 143), and **Group 2**, consisting of patients without PE (n = 138). The table presents key clinical categorical variables as counts and percentages. Statistical significance was assessed using Pearson’s Chi-squared test or Fisher’s Exact test, as appropriate depending on the sample sizes and data distributions. 

To illustrate interpretability, consider the variable **smoking history**. Among patients diagnosed with PE, **26% reported a history of smoking**, while **74% did not.** In contrast, among patients without PE, **29% were smokers** and **71% were non-smokers.** The **p-value for smoking history is 0.6**, indicating **no statistically significant** difference in smoking status between individuals with and without PE. This p-value reflects the result of a Chi-squared test, which evaluates whether the observed distribution of smoking status differs meaningfully between the two groups (whether the proportions of smokers and non-smokers in the PE-positive and PE-negative groups differ beyond what would be expected by chance).

In contrast, when examining the variable **dvt_in_lower_extremity**, a notable difference emerges between groups. Among patients diagnosed with PE, **38% reported having experienced deep vein thrombosis (DVT)** in the lower extremities, while **62% did not.** In comparison, among patients without PE, **14% had experienced DVT**, whereas **86% had not.** The **p-value for this variable is <0.001,** indicating a **statistically significant difference** in the occurrence of lower extremity DVT between individuals with and without PE. This very low p-value suggests that the distribution of DVT status differs meaningfully between the two groups and that the proportions of individuals with and without DVT in the PE-positive and PE-negative groups are unlikely to be due to chance.

While further validation may be warranted, the results of this cross-tabulation suggest that the distribution of the following categorical variables differs significantly between patients with and without pulmonary embolism (PE), supporting their potential clinical relevance in distinguishing PE status: **positive_d_dimer **,  **dvt_in_lower_extremity **,  **pe_more_likely **,  **dvt_pe **,  **septal_bowing **,  **heart_rate_geneva **, **rvsp_based_age**.   

```{r}
cat_summary_table <- merged_data_no_covid %>%
  select(pe_status, all_of(categorical_vars)) %>%
  tbl_summary(
    by = pe_status,
    statistic = list(all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"),
    missing = "no"
  ) %>%
  add_p() %>%
  bold_labels()
cat_summary_table
```

## Continuous Variables: Stratified Analysis 

Bivariate analysis is next conducted on the continuous variables: 

### Statistical Summary Table (Cross-Tabulations)

The table below presents a bivariate analysis comparing continuous clinical variables between patients with pulmonary embolism (PE, n = 143) and those without PE (n = 138). Data are summarized as **mean (standard deviation)**, and comparisons across PE status groups were performed using the **Wilcoxon rank-sum test**, a non-parametric method for comparing two independent groups.

To enhance interpretability, consider the variable **BMI**. Among patients with PE, the **mean BMI is 32**, while among those without PE, the **mean BMI is 31**. The **p-value for BMI is 0.3**, indicating **no statistically significant difference** in BMI between the two groups. Although the mean BMI is slightly higher in the PE group, this small difference is likely due to chance. Therefore, **BMI does not appear to be associated with PE status** in this sample.

In contrast, the variable **d_dimer_value** reveals a more substantial difference. The **mean D-dimer value** among PE-positive patients is **7**, compared to **4** in the non-PE group. The **p-value for this comparison is <0.001**, indicating a **statistically significant difference** between groups. This suggests that the observed difference is unlikely due to chance and reflects a **strong association between elevated D-dimer levels and the presence of PE**. This finding aligns with the known clinical use of D-dimer as a diagnostic biomarker for pulmonary embolism.

While further validation may be warranted, the results from this cross-tabulation suggest that **d_dimer_value**, **echo_rvsp_value**, and **heart_rate** differ significantly between patients with and without PE, supporting their potential clinical relevance in distinguishing PE status.

# Part E (Version 1): Research Objective 1:

> *Investigating which risk factors have a significant association with pulmonary embolism* 

**Note: This analysis was conducted after excluding all patient records from the 2019 admission year.**

To account for the potential confounding effect of the COVID-19 variable, given its absence in 2019, a separate analysis will be performed on the full dataset with the COVID-19 variable removed. The results from both models will be compared to determine whether the same predictors remain statistically significant, thereby assessing the robustness of the findings in relation to the presence or absence of the COVID-19 variable.

Filtering out 2019 data: A total of 76 rows are removed after filtering. There are a total of 281 entries left in the data set.

```{r}
merged_data_no_2019 <- merged_data %>% 
  filter(admission_year != 2019) 
```

## Multivariate Analysis (Logistic Regression) 

The first research question aims to investigate whether a set of clinical and demographic risk factors are significantly associated with the presence of pulmonary embolism (PE), as measured by a binary outcome variable (pe_status: 1 = PE Present and 0 = Pe Absent). 

A total of **25 predictor variables** were included, covering demographic information, imaging findings, and laboratory values. These variables are:

**1. Demographic and Anthropometric Variables: ** 
 - `age_group`, `gender`, `race`, `bmi_marker`, `age`, `bmi`

**2. Pulmonary and Cardiovascular History: ** 
 - `smoking_history`, `copd_history`, `emphysema_ct`, `copd_exacerbation`, `covid`

**3. Laboratory Biomarkers: **
 - `positive_d_dimer`, `d_dimer_value`, `elevated_bnp`, `bnp_levels`, `elevated_troponin`

**4. Vascular and Cardiac Risk Markers: ** 
 - `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, `rvsp_based_age`, `echo_rvsp_value`, `rv_hypokines_on_echo`, `pulmonary_hypertension`, `rh_thrombus`, `rh_strain`, `tricuspid_regurgitation`, `septal_bowing`. 

A logistic regression model was implemented using a **logit link function**, which is appropriate for modeling binary outcome variables such as `pe_status`. The objective of this model is to assess whether each predictor is significantly associated with the likelihood or log odds of developing pulmonary embolism, while adjusting for the influence of all other variables in the model.

The model summary includes the estimated **regression coefficients**, **standard errors**, and **p-values** for each predictor variable, allowing for evaluation of their individual statistical significance. Additionally, the output reports the **null deviance** and **residual deviance** of the model, which indicate the goodness of fit of the null versus fitted model. The **Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) ** is also provided and will be used to comparing alternative models.

Ensure that PE = 0 is the reference group: 

```{r}
merged_data_no_2019$pe_status <- factor(merged_data_no_2019$pe_status, levels = c(0, 1))
contrasts(merged_data_no_2019$pe_status)
```

```{r}
first_predictors <- c("age_group", "age", "bmi", "gender", "bmi_marker", "race", 
                      "smoking_history", "copd_history", "emphysema_ct", 
                      "copd_exacerbation", "positive_d_dimer", "d_dimer_value", 
                      "covid", "elevated_bnp", "bnp_levels", "elevated_troponin", 
                      "dvt_in_lower_extremity", "rvsp_based_age", "echo_rvsp_value", 
                      "rv_hypokines_on_echo", "pulmonary_hypertension", 
                      "rh_strain", "tricuspid_regurgitation", "septal_bowing", "rh_thrombus")

formula_string <- paste("pe_status ~", paste(first_predictors, collapse = " + "))
l_model <- glm(as.formula(formula_string), family = binomial, data = merged_data_no_2019)
```

```{r}
lmod_sm <- summary(l_model) 
lmod_sm
```

According to the model summary, the most statistically significant predictors of pulmonary embolism in the logistic regression model are `positive_d_dimer`, `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, and `echo_rvsp_value`. Before proceeding to formal model validation, it is important to assess the model for potential issues such as **perfect separation** and **multicollinearity** among the predictor variables. It is also noted that this represents the **initial model fitting**, and the issue of **overfitting** will be addressed in subsequent stages of the analysis.

## Need for Data Diagnostics: 

### Perfect Separation Check
The model is evaluated for perfect separation, a condition in which a predictor variable perfectly predicts the outcome. This scenario can lead to inflated standard errors, unstable coefficient estimates, and model convergence issues.

- `rh_thrombus`: From the model summary, the coefficient estimate has high standard error (7.815e+02), suggesting perfect separation. From the cross-tabulation below, no individuals with a right heart thrombus were observed in the PE-negative group (all such cases occurred in PE-positive patients). This lack of overlap leads to perfect separation, destabilizing the model.

- `race`: The cross-tabulation shows that certain race categories (category 5) have zero cases in the PE-positive group. This again results in separation, as the model cannot estimate a reliable effect when one category does not co-occur with both outcome levels. In addition, when examining the distribution of the the different values of `race` when stratified between patients with pulmonary embolism and without in the stacked bar graphs above, there are 0 entries of patients in the Other category who have pulmonary embolism, causing the perfect separation. 

```{r}
cat("Cross-tabulation: Race vs PE Status\n")
race_tab <- table(merged_data_no_2019$race, merged_data_no_2019$pe_status)
colnames(race_tab) <- c("PE = 0", "PE = 1")
print(race_tab)

cat("\nCross-tabulation: RH Thrombus vs PE Status\n")
thrombus_tab <- table(merged_data_no_2019$rh_thrombus, merged_data_no_2019$pe_status)
colnames(thrombus_tab) <- c("PE = 0", "PE = 1")
print(thrombus_tab)
```

To resolve **perfect separation**, we combine the `Other` (6) and `Indian-American` (5) categories within the `race` variable into a single, category. This adjustment ensures that all race categories have representation in both the PE-positive and PE-negative groups, allowing for more stable coefficient estimates.

```{r}
merged_data_no_2019$race<- merged_data_no_2019$race
merged_data_no_2019$race[merged_data_no_2019$race == 6] <- 5
```

In addition, the variable `rh_thrombus` will be deleted as a predictor variable from the logistic regression model. 

### Multicollinearity: 

To reduce multicollinearity, we removed the variables `age_group` and `bmi` from the model, as they were highly correlated with their numerical or categorical counterparts, `age` and `bmi_marker`, respectively. Including both continuous and categorical forms of the same variable in a logistic regression model can distort coefficient estimates and inflate standard errors.

The variables `d_dimer_value` and `bnp_levels`, both continuous measures, were excluded to avoid redundancy with their corresponding binary indicators, `positive_d_dimer` and `elevated_bnp`, respectively. Additionally, the categorical variable `rvsp_based_age` was excluded due to its correlation with its continuous counterpart, `echo_rvsp_value`.

As a result, a total of 19 predictor variables in the final logistic regression model will be used.  

```{r}
new_predictors <- c("age", "gender", "bmi_marker", "race", 
                      "smoking_history", "copd_history", "emphysema_ct", 
                      "copd_exacerbation", "positive_d_dimer",
                      "covid", "elevated_bnp", "elevated_troponin", 
                      "dvt_in_lower_extremity", "echo_rvsp_value", 
                      "rv_hypokines_on_echo", "pulmonary_hypertension", 
                      "rh_strain", "tricuspid_regurgitation", "septal_bowing") 

new_formula_string <- paste("pe_status ~", paste(new_predictors, collapse = " + "))
new_model <- glm(as.formula(new_formula_string), family = binomial, data = merged_data_no_2019)
summary(new_model) 
```

To further assess multicollinearity, the **Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) ** was examined for all predictors. All VIF values were found to be below 5, indicating that no severe multicollinearity is present among the variables included in the model.

```{r}
vif_results <- car::vif(new_model)
print(vif_results)
```

### Interpretation of Coefficients (Log Odds): 

The table below presents the results of the logistic regression model after addressing issues of perfect separation and multicollinearity among predictors. Each row displays the estimated **log odds ratio**, the corresponding **95% confidence interval**, and the **p-value** assessing the statistical significance of each clinical predictor. A total of 19 variables were included in the model to evaluate their potential association with the likelihood of pulmonary embolism.

Interpreting in terms of **log odds** of developing pulmonary embolism: 

1. `positive_d_dimer`: Individuals with an elevated level of D-dimer in the blood (≥ 0.50 µg/mL FEU or 500 ng/mL) have higher log-odds of developing pulmonary embolism compared to those without elevated D-dimer levels, with an estimated difference of  2.59703 units, holding all other predictors constant. This association is statistically significant (p-value = 0.00509), indicating that elevated D-dimer levels contribute meaningfully to the model and are associated with an increased likelihood of PE. 

2. `dvt_in_lower_extremity`: Patients with deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the lower extremities have 1.67335 units higher log-odds of having pulmonary embolism (PE) compared to those without DVT. This coefficient is highly statistically significant (p-value = 2.4 × 10⁻⁶), indicating a strong and clinically consistent association between DVT and PE.

3. `echo_rvsp_value`: Individuals with higher right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) value have 0.03341 units higher log-odds of developing pulmonary embolism compared to those with lower right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) value, holding all other predictors constant. This coefficient is statistically significant (p-value = 0.00018), suggesting a meaningful association between elevated RVSP and the presence of pulmonary embolism.


```{r}
new_model %>% 
  tbl_regression() %>%
  bold_labels() %>%
  bold_p(t = 0.05)
```

## Confidence Intervals 

To assess the precision of the coefficient estimates, **95% confidence intervals ** were computed for each predicor using the `confint()` function. The intervals provide a range of possible values for the true log odds of developing pulmonary embolism with respect to the designated variables. 

Interpretations of the 95 percent confidence intervals for the three most singificnat predictors in the logistic regression model: 

- `positive_d_dimer`: 

**95% Confidence Interval (0.99214595, 4.73335019) **
The interval indicates that the log-odds of developing pulmonary embolism are between **0.99 and 4.73 units higher ** for individuals with a positive D-dimer result compared to those without, assuming all other predictor variables are held constant. Since the entire interval lies above zero, this suggests a statistically **significant positive association**, indicating that a positive D-dimer result is **strongly associated with increased log-odds or odds** of developing pulmonary embolism.

- `dvt_in_lower_extremity`: 

**95% Confidence Interval (1.00019550, 2.39768007) **
The interval indicates that the log-odds of developing pulmonary embolism are between **1.00019550 and 2.39768007 units higher ** for individuals with documented DVT in the lower extremity compared to those without, assuming all other predictor variables are held constant. Since the entire interval lies above zero, this suggests a statistically **significant positive association**, indicating that DVT presence is **strongly associated with increased log-odds or odds** of developing pulmonary embolism.

- `echo_rvsp_value`:

**95% Confidence Interval (0.01650554, 0.05166404) **
The interval indicates that for every one unit increase in RVSP (right ventricular systolic pressure), the log-odds of developing pulmonary embolism increases by between **0.01650554 and 0.05166404 units **, assuming all other predictor variables are held constant. Since the entire interval lies above zero, this suggests a statistically **significant positive association**, indicating that higher right ventricular systolic pressure is **strongly associated with increased log-odds or odds** of developing pulmonary embolism.

```{r}
confint(new_model)
```

### Interpretation of Coefficients (Odds): 

Interpreting in terms of **Odds** of developing pulmonary embolism: 

1. `positive_d_dimer`: Individuals with an elevated level of d-dimer in the blood (0.50ug/mL FEU or 500 ng/mL) has higher odds of developing pulmonary embolism compared to individuals who do not have an elevated level of d-dimer in the blood by a factor of 13.4 units, holding other predictors constant. 

2. `dvt_in_lower_extremity`: Patients with deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the lower extremities has 5.33 units higher odds of having PE compared to those without DVT, holding other predictors constant. 

3. `echo_rvsp_value`: Individuals with higher RVSP value (right ventricular systolic presssure) value have higher odds of developing pulmonary embolsim compared to individuals with a low RVSP value by a factor of 1.03, holding other predictors constant.

```{r}
new_model%>%
  tbl_regression(intercept = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  bold_labels() %>%
  bold_p(t = 0.05)
```


## Inference (Analysis of Deviance) 

### Validation Method#1: Null Model versus Fitted Model: 

To evaluate the overall fit of the logistic regression model, the **deviance values** of the null model (with no predictors) and the fitted model (with predictors) were compared. The **difference in deviance** between the two models is **76.54839**, which serves as the test statistic for a **likelihood ratio test.**

This test evaluates the null hypothesis that the **null model provides a better fit** to the data compared to the fitted model. The **alternative hypothesis** is that the **fitted model**, which includes the predictor variables, offers a significantly better fit.

The resulting **p-value is 7.060734e-07**, which is well below the standard significance threshold of 0.05. This provides strong evidence to **reject the null hypothesis**, indicating that the fitted model explains the data significantly better than the null model. Therefore, the inclusion of the predictor variables improves the model's ability to capture variability in pulmonary embolism status.

```{r}
test_statistic <- new_model$null.deviance - new_model$deviance
test_statistic
```

```{r}
pchisq(test_statistic, 26, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

### Validation Method #2: Drop_1 Function 
The results of the likelihood ratio test using the `drop1()` function evaluate the individual contribution of each predictor to the logistic regression model by measuring the change in model deviance upon its removal. An increase in deviance after removing a variable indicates that the predictor plays a meaningful role in explaining variability in the outcome variable, `pe_status`, and therefore should be retained in the model. Notably, the variables `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, `positive_d_dimer`, and `echo_rvsp_value` exhibit statistically significant contributions, as their exclusion results in substantial increases in model deviance (324.46, 338.37, and 328.58, respectively). These increases correspond to highly significant p-values, suggesting that these predictors meaningfully enhance model fit. This reinforces earlier findings that these three variables are important determinants of pulmonary embolism in the dataset and should be preserved in the final model.

```{r}
drop1(new_model, test = "Chi")
```

### Validation Method #3: Likelihood Ratio Test: 

To further support the importance of the three key predictor variables, their individual contributions were evaluated using an analysis of deviance approach. Specifically, likelihood ratio tests were conducted to compare the full logistic regression model with reduced models that exclude each respective predictor. This method assesses whether the removal of a given variable results in a significantly poorer model fit, thereby justifying its inclusion.

- Is the predictor `dvt_in_lower_extremity` necessary in the model? 

The analysis of deviance table below compares the full logistic regression model, which includes the predictor `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, with a reduced model in which this variable is excluded. The likelihood ratio test evaluates whether removing the variable significantly worsens the model fit. The results show a deviance difference of 25.458 with 1 degree of freedom and a corresponding p-value of 4.521e-07. This extremely low p-value indicates that the reduced model fits the data significantly worse than the full model. Therefore, `dvt_in_lower_extremity` contributes meaningful explanatory value to the model and should be retained as an important predictor of pulmonary embolism.

```{r}
reduced_predictors <- setdiff(new_predictors, "dvt_in_lower_extremity")
reduced_formula <- as.formula(paste("pe_status ~", paste(reduced_predictors, collapse = " + ")))
reduced_dvt <- glm(reduced_formula, family = binomial, data = merged_data_no_2019)
anova(reduced_dvt, new_model, test = "Chi")
```

- Is the predictor `echo_rvsp_value` necessary in the model? 

The analysis of deviance table below compares the full logistic regression model, which includes the predictor `echo_rvsp_value`, with a reduced model in which this variable is excluded. The results show a deviance difference of 15.672 with 1 degree of freedom and a corresponding p-value of 7.533e-05. This extremely low p-value indicates that the reduced model fits the data significantly worse than the full model. Therefore, `echo_rvsp_value` contributes meaningful explanatory value to the model and should be retained as an important predictor of pulmonary embolism.

```{r}
reduced_predictors <- setdiff(new_predictors, "echo_rvsp_value")
reduced_formula <- as.formula(paste("pe_status ~", paste(reduced_predictors, collapse = " + ")))
reduced_rvsp <- glm(reduced_formula, family = binomial, data = merged_data_no_2019)
anova(reduced_rvsp, new_model, test = "Chi")
```

- Is the predictor `positive_d_dimer`  necessary in the model? 

The analysis of deviance table below compares the full logistic regression model, which includes the predictor `positive_d_dimer`, with a reduced model in which this variable is excluded. The results show a deviance difference of 11.547 with 1 degree of freedom and a corresponding p-value of 0.0006786. This extremely low p-value indicates that the reduced model fits the data significantly worse than the full model. Therefore, `positive_d_dimer` contributes meaningful explanatory value to the model and should be retained as an important predictor of pulmonary embolism.

```{r}
reduced_predictors <- setdiff(new_predictors, "positive_d_dimer")
reduced_formula <- as.formula(paste("pe_status ~", paste(reduced_predictors, collapse = " + ")))
reduced_d_dimer <- glm(reduced_formula, family = binomial, data = merged_data_no_2019)
anova(reduced_d_dimer, new_model, test = "Chi")
```


**Summary of Results Pertaining to Analysis of Deviance **

Based on the results of the analysis of deviance and likelihood ratio tests, the following three predictor variables: `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, `positive_d_dimer`, and `echo_rvsp_value` all demonstrate statistically significant contributions to the logistic regression model for predicting pulmonary embolism (PE).

In **Method #1: LRT between Null and Fitted Models**, the comparison between the full model (with predictors) and the null model (without predictors) shows that the full model provides a significantly better fit to the observed data. The likelihood ratio test yields a p-value of **7.060734e-07**, indicating that the overall model is statistically meaningful and that the inclusion of predictors improves model performance.

In **Method #2: Drop_1 function**, the `drop1()` function is used to evaluate the impact of removing each predictor from the model. The removal of `dvt_in_lower_extremity` results in the largest increase in deviance (**25.4579**, p-value = **4.521e-07**), highlighting its strong explanatory value. Similarly, `positive_d_dimer` and `echo_rvsp_value` also show significant increases in deviance when excluded (**11.547** and **15.672**, respectively), with p-values below the conventional 0.05 threshold. These results confirm that each of the three variables contributes meaningfully to the model’s fit.

In **Method #3: Individual Likelihodo Ratio Tests**, individual likelihood ratio tests further confirm the importance of these predictors by comparing the full model to reduced models with each respective variable excluded. All three tests return small p-values, indicating that excluding any of these variables leads to a significantly worse model fit.

Together, these validation methods provide robust support for the inclusion of `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, `positive_d_dimer`, and `echo_rvsp_value` as important predictors of pulmonary embolism status in the logistic regression model. Furthermore, the relative importance of these predictors can be ranked as follows: `dvt_in_lower_extremity` > `echo_rvsp_value`> `positive_d_dimer`. However, further diagnostic evaluation is warranted and will be conducted in the next steps of the analysis to confirm these findings and ensure model stability.

## Residual Diagnostics 

To evaluate the goodness of fit of the logistic regression model with 19 predictor variables, residual diagnostics were conducted using both the raw and deviance residuals. This is an additional way to validate the selction of the three most significant predictors. 

```{r}
linpred  <- predict(new_model)
linpred %>% head(10)
```

```{r}
predprob <- predict(new_model, type = "response")
predprob %>% head(10)
```

```{r}
rawres <- new_model$y - predprob
```

### Raw Residuals 

The **raw residuals** were calculated as the difference between the observed binary outcomes (`y`) and the predicted probabilities (`ŷ`) from the full logistic regression model. A scatterplot of the raw residuals against the linear predictor (log-odds) was generated; however, this plot is not particularly informative. As expected in logistic regression, the residuals clustered into two distinct bands - one corresponding to observations with an outcome of 0 and the other to those with an outcome of 1. Due to this limited interpretability, **deviance residuals** were computed instead. These standardized residuals are more appropriate for evaluating model fit in logistic regression, as they account for the binary nature of the outcome and provide a clearer indication of discrepancies between observed and predicted values.

```{r}
merged_data_no_2019 %>%
  mutate(rawres = rawres, linpred = linpred) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = linpred, y = rawres)) +
  labs(x = "Linear predictor", y = "Raw residuals")
```

### Deviance Residuals 

Deviance residuals are standardized residuals that differ from raw residuals in that they account for the variance structure of binary outcomes in logistic regression. They measure the contribution of each individual observation to the overall model deviance by comparing the fitted model to a saturated model, which perfectly fits the data. When plotted against the linear predictor, the deviance residuals cluster again into two distinct lines where one corresponds to yi = 0 and the other one corresponds to yi = 1. 

To enhance the interpretability of the residual diagnostics and reduce visual noise, binned deviance residuals are computed by dividing the range of the linear predictor into 20 quantile-based bins and calculating the average residual within each bin. This approach is implemented in the next graph. 

```{r}
devres <- residuals(new_model)
devres %>% head(10) 
```

```{r}
sqrt(-2 * (new_model$y * log(predprob) + (1 - new_model$y) * log(1 - predprob))) %>%
  head(10)
```


```{r}
merged_data_no_2019 %>%
  mutate(devres = devres, linpred = linpred) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = linpred, y = devres)) +
  labs(x = "Linear predictor", y = "Deviance residuals")
```

### Binned Deviance Residuals 

The final binned residual plot includes a red horizontal dashed line at 0, representing perfect model fit. The size of each point reflects the number of observations within the corresponding bin of the linear predictor. As the binned deviance residuals are randomly scattered around this reference line with no discernible systematic pattern, the model appears to be reasonably well specified. This supports the validity of the statistical inferences made regarding the significance of the identified predictors, `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, `echo_rvsp_value`, and `positive_d_dimer`. 

```{r}
merged_data_no_2019 %>%
  mutate(devres = devres, linpred = linpred) %>% 
  group_by(cut(linpred, breaks = unique(quantile(linpred, (1:20)/21)))) %>%
  summarize(devres = mean(devres), 
            linpred = mean(linpred),
            n = n()) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = linpred, y = devres, size = n)) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Linear predictor", y = "Binned deviance residual",
       title = "Binned Deviance Residuals", 
       subtitle = "Red line at y=0 indicates good fit",
       size = "Number of observations") +
  theme_minimal()
```


**NOTE**: This concludes the analysis for the first research question using the dataset that excludes all patients admitted in 2019. In this model, the three predictors found to be statistically significant were `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, `echo_rvsp_value`, and `positive_d_dimer`. Since `COVID-19` did not emerge as a significant predictor, it can be inferred that its presence does not substantially influence the relationship between admission year and pulmonary embolism status.

Accordingly, the subsequent analysis addressing the same research question will use the full dataset (including 2019 admissions), but will exclude the COVID-19 variable to maintain consistency and avoid temporal confounding.

# Part E (Version 2): Research Objective 1: Association between Risk Factors and Pulmonary Embolism  

## Multivariate Analysis (Logistic Regression) 

The first research question aims to investigate whether a set of clinical and demographic risk factors are significantly associated with the presence of pulmonary embolism (PE), as measured by a binary outcome variable (pe_status: 1 = PE Present and 0 = Pe Absent). 

A total of **24 predictor variables** were included, covering demographic information, imaging findings, and laboratory values. These variables are:

**1. Demographic and Anthropometric Variables: ** 
 - `age_group`, `gender`, `race`, `bmi_marker`, `age`, `bmi`

**2. Pulmonary and Cardiovascular History: ** 
 - `smoking_history`, `copd_history`, `emphysema_ct`, `copd_exacerbation`

**3. Laboratory Biomarkers: **
 - `positive_d_dimer`, `d_dimer_value`, `elevated_bnp`, `bnp_levels`, `elevated_troponin`

**4. Vascular and Cardiac Risk Markers: ** 
 - `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, `rvsp_based_age`, `echo_rvsp_value`, `rv_hypokines_on_echo`, `pulmonary_hypertension`, `rh_thrombus`, `rh_strain`, `tricuspid_regurgitation`, `septal_bowing`. 

A logistic regression model was implemented using a **logit link function**, which is appropriate for modeling binary outcome variables such as `pe_status`. The objective of this model is to assess whether each predictor is significantly associated with the likelihood or log odds of developing pulmonary embolism, while adjusting for the influence of all other variables in the model.

The model summary includes the estimated **regression coefficients**, **standard errors**, and **p-values** for each predictor variable, allowing for evaluation of their individual statistical significance. Additionally, the output reports the **null deviance** and **residual deviance** of the model, which indicate the goodness of fit of the null versus fitted model. The **Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) ** is also provided and will be used to comparing alternative models.

Ensure that PE = 0 is the reference group: 

```{r}
merged_data_no_covid$pe_status <- factor(merged_data_no_covid$pe_status, levels = c(0, 1))
contrasts(merged_data_no_covid$pe_status)
```

```{r}
first_predictors <- c("age_group", "age", "bmi", "gender", "bmi_marker", "race", 
                      "smoking_history", "copd_history", "emphysema_ct", 
                      "copd_exacerbation", "positive_d_dimer", "d_dimer_value", 
                      "elevated_bnp", "bnp_levels", "elevated_troponin", 
                      "dvt_in_lower_extremity", "rvsp_based_age", "echo_rvsp_value", 
                      "rv_hypokines_on_echo", "pulmonary_hypertension", 
                      "rh_strain", "tricuspid_regurgitation", "septal_bowing", "rh_thrombus")

formula_string <- paste("pe_status ~", paste(first_predictors, collapse = " + "))
l_model_new <- glm(as.formula(formula_string), family = binomial, data = merged_data_no_covid)
```

```{r}
lmod_sm_new <- summary(l_model_new) 
lmod_sm_new
```

According to the model summary, the most statistically significant predictors of pulmonary embolism in the logistic regression model are `positive_d_dimer`, `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, and `echo_rvsp_value`. Before proceeding to formal model validation, it is important to assess the model for potential issues such as **perfect separation** and **multicollinearity** among the predictor variables. It is also noted that this represents the **initial model fitting**, and the issue of **overfitting** will be addressed in subsequent stages of the analysis.

## Need for Data Diagnostics: 

### Perfect Separation Check
The model is evaluated for perfect separation, a condition in which a predictor variable perfectly predicts the outcome. This scenario can lead to inflated standard errors, unstable coefficient estimates, and model convergence issues.

- `rh_thrombus`: From the model summary, the coefficient estimate has high standard error (7.815e+02), suggesting perfect separation. From the cross-tabulation below, no individuals with a right heart thrombus were observed in the PE-negative group (all such cases occurred in PE-positive patients). This lack of overlap leads to perfect separation, destabilizing the model.

- `race`: The cross-tabulation shows that certain race categories (category 5) have zero cases in the PE-positive group. This again results in separation, as the model cannot estimate a reliable effect when one category does not co-occur with both outcome levels. In addition, when examining the distribution of the the different values of `race` when stratified between patients with pulmonary embolism and without in the stacked bar graphs above, there are 0 entries of patients in the Other category who have pulmonary embolism, causing the perfect separation. 

```{r}
cat("Cross-tabulation: Race vs PE Status\n")
race_tab <- table(merged_data_no_covid$race,merged_data_no_covid $pe_status)
colnames(race_tab) <- c("PE = 0", "PE = 1")
print(race_tab)

cat("\nCross-tabulation: RH Thrombus vs PE Status\n")
thrombus_tab <- table(merged_data_no_covid $rh_thrombus, merged_data_no_covid$pe_status)
colnames(thrombus_tab) <- c("PE = 0", "PE = 1")
print(thrombus_tab)
```

To resolve **perfect separation**, we combine the `Other` (6) and `Indian-American` (5) categories within the `race` variable into a single, category. This adjustment ensures that all race categories have representation in both the PE-positive and PE-negative groups, allowing for more stable coefficient estimates.

```{r}
merged_data_no_covid$race<- merged_data_no_covid$race
merged_data_no_covid$race[merged_data_no_covid$race == 6] <- 5
```

In addition, the variable `rh_thrombus` will be deleted as a predictor variable from the logistic regression model. 

### Multicollinearity: 

To reduce multicollinearity, we removed the variables `age_group` and `bmi` from the model, as they were highly correlated with their numerical or categorical counterparts, `age` and `bmi_marker`, respectively. Including both continuous and categorical forms of the same variable in a logistic regression model can distort coefficient estimates and inflate standard errors.

The variables `d_dimer_value` and `bnp_levels`, both continuous measures, were excluded to avoid redundancy with their corresponding binary indicators, `positive_d_dimer` and `elevated_bnp`, respectively. Additionally, the categorical variable `rvsp_based_age` was excluded due to its correlation with its continuous counterpart, `echo_rvsp_value`.

As a result, a total of 18 predictor variables in the final logistic regression model will be used.  

```{r}
new_predictors <- c("age", "gender", "bmi_marker", "race", 
                      "smoking_history", "copd_history", "emphysema_ct", 
                      "copd_exacerbation", "positive_d_dimer",
                      "elevated_bnp", "elevated_troponin", 
                      "dvt_in_lower_extremity", "echo_rvsp_value", 
                      "rv_hypokines_on_echo", "pulmonary_hypertension", 
                      "rh_strain", "tricuspid_regurgitation", "septal_bowing") 

new_formula_string <- paste("pe_status ~", paste(new_predictors, collapse = " + "))
new_model_no_covid <- glm(as.formula(new_formula_string), family = binomial, data = merged_data_no_covid )
summary(new_model_no_covid) 
```

To further assess multicollinearity, the **Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) ** was examined for all predictors. All VIF values were found to be below 5, indicating that no severe multicollinearity is present among the variables included in the model.

```{r}
vif_results <- car::vif(new_model_no_covid)
print(vif_results)
```

### Interpretation of Coefficients (Log Odds): 

The table below presents the results of the logistic regression model after addressing issues of perfect separation and multicollinearity among predictors. Each row displays the estimated **log odds ratio**, the corresponding **95% confidence interval**, and the **p-value** assessing the statistical significance of each clinical predictor. A total of 19 variables were included in the model to evaluate their potential association with the likelihood of pulmonary embolism.

Interpreting in terms of **log odds** of developing pulmonary embolism: 

1. `positive_d_dimer`: Individuals with an elevated level of D-dimer in the blood (≥ 0.50 µg/mL FEU or 500 ng/mL) have higher log-odds of developing pulmonary embolism compared to those without elevated D-dimer levels, with an estimated difference of 2.106436 units, holding all other predictors constant. This association is statistically significant (p-value = 0.00404), indicating that elevated D-dimer levels contribute meaningfully to the model and are associated with an increased likelihood of PE. 

2. `dvt_in_lower_extremity`: Patients with deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the lower extremities have 1.308595 units higher log-odds of having pulmonary embolism (PE) compared to those without DVT. This coefficient is highly statistically significant (p-value = 8.36e-06), indicating a strong and clinically consistent association between DVT and PE.

3. `echo_rvsp_value`: Individuals with higher right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) value have 0.036138 units higher log-odds of developing pulmonary embolism compared to those with lower right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) value, holding all other predictors constant. This coefficient is statistically significant (p-value = 2.60e-06), suggesting a meaningful association between elevated RVSP and the presence of pulmonary embolism.

```{r}
  bold_labels() %>%
```
