**Conclusion: ** 

Overall, incorporating select socioeconomic, behavioral, and social determinant predictors (particularly food_insecurity, income_poverty_ratio, and citizenship_status that proved to be significant predictors of diabetes in earlier analysis) enhanced model fit as evidenced by improved AIC and pseudo-R² values, without significantly reducing classifcation performance. Although none of the expanded models substantially outperform the ADA baseline in out-of-sample classification performance, the improvements in model fit are statistically meaningful. Specifically, the ADA + income_poverty_ratio + citizenship_status + food_insecurity model achieved the strongest overall fit (ΔAIC = −25.35; ΔR² = +0.0047) while maintaining comparable classification metrics (AUC = 0.8060 vs 0.8057, Accuracy = 0.6728 vs 0.6840, Sensitivity = 0.8330 vs 0.8196, Specificity = 0.6477 vs 0.6628). Taken together, this model offers the best balance between improved fit, predictive stability, and parsimony, supporting its selection as the most effective enhancement to the ADA Diabetes Risk Test.








#HELLLOOOO 


## Scoring System #2: Modified Geneva Score 

In this part of the analysis, we will evaluate whether incorporating the three significant variables (`positive_d_dimer`, `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, and `echo_rvsp_value`) into the current Modified Geneva Scoring System meaningfully improves its overall performance in terms of model fit and predictive performance. Model fit was assessed using AIC, BIC, and penalized deviance, while predictive performance was evaluated in terms of both discrimination (Area Under the ROC Curve, AUC), classification accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and overall accuracy), and calibration performance (how well the predicted probabilities match real world outcome frequencies). The analysis also aimed to identify the most parsimonious subset of these additional predictors that provides the optimal balance between model fit, predictive performance, and simplicity for practical screening for pulmonary embolism.


**Original Variables in the Modified Geneva Scoring System:** 
- 1. `age_greater_65`: Age > 65 years old - 1 point 
- 2. `dvt_pe`: Previous deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism - 3 points
- 3. `surgery_fracture`: Surgery under general anesthesia or fracture of the lower limbs within one month - 2 points
- 4. `active_malignancy`: Active malignancy (solid or hematologic; currently active or cured within the last year) - 2 points 
- 5. `unilateral_lower_limb_pain`: Symptoms Unilateral lower-limb pain - 3 points 
- 6.  `haemoptysis`: Haemoptysis - 2 points 
- 7.  `heart_rate_geneva`: Signs Heart Rate: (75-94 beats per minute) - 3 points or (greater than or equal to 95 beats per minute) - 4 points 
- 8. `pain_lower_limb_edema`: Pain on lower limb deep venous palpation and unilateral oedema - 4 points 

**Interpretation of Modified Geneva Score:** 

- *Pretest Probability assessment Low*: **(0-3 points)**
- *Intermediate:* **(4-10 points)**
- *High:* **(greater than or equal to 11 points)** 

### Logistic Model Fitting (Modified Geneva Scoring System)
> *Does adding all three significant predictors improve the model fit and predictive performance of the original Modified Wells diagnostic scoring system?*

Fitting Logistic Regression Model with Original Predictors: To evaluate the overall performance of the original **Modified Geneva Score**, a logistic regression model was fitted with the binary outcome variable `pe_status` (presence or absence of pulmonary embolism) regressed on the eight original predictors that comprise the **Modified Geneva criteria.**

```{r}
merged_data_no_covid

geneva_components <- c("age_greater_65", "dvt_pe", "surgery_fracture", "active_malignancy", "unilateral_lower_limb_pain", "haemoptysis", "heart_rate_geneva", "pain_lower_limb_edema") 

colnames(merged_data_no_covid)

model_geneva_original <- glm(pe_status ~ .,
                     data = merged_data_no_covid[, c("pe_status", geneva_components)],
                     family = binomial)
```

3 significant predictors: `dvt_in_lower_extremity`, `echo_rvsp_value`, and `positive_d_dimer` 
 
Fitting Logistic Regression Model with Additional Predictors: To evaluate whether incorporating additional statistically significant predictors improves the overall performance of the original Modified Geneva Score, the original model was expanded to include three additional variables: `echo_rvsp_value`, `positive_d_dimer`, and `dvt_in_lower_extremity`. 

```{r}
enhanced_geneva_predictors <- c(geneva_components, "positive_d_dimer", "echo_rvsp_value", "dvt_in_lower_extremity")
enhanced_geneva_predictors <- unique(enhanced_geneva_predictors)

model_geneva_enhanced <- glm(pe_status ~ .,
                     data = merged_data_no_covid[, c("pe_status", enhanced_geneva_predictors)], 
                     family = binomial)
```

Before conducting the likelihood ratio test to compare the two nested logistic regression models, both **perfect separation** and **multicollinearity** were assessed to ensure model validity. In examining perfect separation, the variable `haemoptysis` was identified as problematic (which was already established when constructing the Modified Wells model). As a result, a bias-reduced logistic regression model, also known as **Firth’s logistic regression**, was employed to address the issue of perfect separation. The variable `haemoptysis` was retained in the model despite perfect separation because it represents a clinically essential component of the original Modified Geneva Score diagnostic criteria.

```{r}
for (var in enhanced_geneva_predictors) {
  cat("Checking separation for:", var, "\n")
  print(table(merged_data_no_covid[[var]], merged_data_no_covid$pe_status, useNA = "ifany"))
}
```

The summary of the Firth Regression model for the Original Modified Geneva Score Model is as follows: 

```{r}
model_geneva_original_firth <- logistf(pe_status ~ .,
                                     data = merged_data_no_covid[, c("pe_status", geneva_components)])
summary(model_geneva_original_firth)
```

The summary of the Firth Regression model for the Enhanced Modified Geneva Score Model (including three more parameters) is as follows: 

```{r}
model_geneva_enhanced_firth <- logistf(pe_status ~ .,
                                     data = merged_data_no_covid[, c("pe_status", enhanced_geneva_predictors)])
summary(model_geneva_enhanced_firth)
```

Next, **multicollinearity** among predictors was assessed for both the original and enhanced models. Although Firth’s logistic regression was used to address perfect separation, this bias-corrected approach does not alter the relationships among predictors. Therefore, multicollinearity was evaluated using the corresponding standard logistic regression models.

All Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) values were below 5, indicating that no strong multicollinearity was present among the wells predictors in the model. This suggests that the estimated regression coefficients are stable and not inflated due to redundant information between variables.

```{r}
vif_results <- car::vif(model_geneva_original)
print(vif_results)
```

All Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) values were below 5, indicating that no strong multicollinearity was present among the wells predictors, as well as `positive_d_dimer` and `echo_rvsp_value` in the model. This suggests that the estimated regression coefficients are stable and not inflated due to redundant information between variables.

```{r}
vif_results <- car::vif(model_geneva_enhanced)
print(vif_results)
```

Likelihood ratio tests comparing the reduced and full models are next performed after detecting perfect separation and then addressing it by using Firth's penalized logistic regression along with assessing multicollinearity. 

### Statistical Comparison: Likelihood Ratio Test between Reduced and Full Model (after adding 3 new predictors) 

A likelihood ratio test was conducted to compare two nested Firth's penalized logistic regression models. The null hypothesis states that the reduced model, which includes only the original **Modified Geneva Score** predictors, provides an adequate fit to the data. The alternative hypothesis suggests that the extended model, which includes the original predictors plus three additional variables, offers a significantly better fit. 

The test produced a test statistic value of **30.6026** on 2 degrees of freedom and a **p-value of 0.000000226**, indicating strong evidence against the null hypothesis. Therefore, it can be concluded that adding the predictors `positive_d_dimer`, `echo_rvsp_value`, and `dvt_in_lower_extremity` significantly improves the model's ability to explain significant additional variation in pulmonary embolism status beyond what the predictors of the original Modified Geneva Score alone explains. This suggests that the full model provides a better fit to the in-sample data compared to the original Modified Geneva Score model. 

```{r}
ll_original  <- model_geneva_original_firth$loglik["full"]
ll_enhanced  <- model_geneva_enhanced_firth$loglik["full"]

lr_stat <- 2 * (ll_enhanced - ll_original)

df_diff <- (length(coef(model_geneva_enhanced_firth)) -
            length(coef(model_geneva_original_firth)))  

p_value <- pchisq(lr_stat, df = df_diff, lower.tail = FALSE)

cat(sprintf("Penalized LRT: χ²(%d) = %.4f, p = %.9f\n",
            df_diff, lr_stat, p_value))
```

### Statistical Comparison: Model Selection Criteria: Penalized Log-likelihood, Penalized Deviance, AIC, BIC 

**Model Selection Criteria #1: Penalized Log-Likelihood and Penalized Deviance ** 

To further compare model fit between the two Firth logistic regression models, we examined the **penalized deviance**, defined as −2 times the fitted penalized log-likelihood. Penalized deviance was **307.20** for the original Modified Geneva model and **276.59** for the enhanced model. The deviance difference (original − enhanced) was **30.60**, indicating that the enhanced model achieves a substantially lower penalized deviance (better in-sample fit) under the Firth penalized likelihood. This result is consistent with the earlier penalized likelihood ratio test showing improved fit after adding `positive_d_dimer`, `echo_rvsp_value`, and `dvt_in_lower_extremity`. 

```{r}
ll_orig <- model_geneva_original_firth$loglik["full"]
ll_enh  <- model_geneva_enhanced_firth$loglik["full"]

deviance_original <- -2 * ll_orig
deviance_enhanced  <- -2 * ll_enh

model_comparison_deviance <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Reduced (Original Geneva, Firth)",
            "Full (Enhanced Geneva, Firth)",
            "Difference (Original - Enhanced)"),
  Deviance = round(c(
    as.numeric(deviance_original),
    as.numeric(deviance_enhanced),
    as.numeric(deviance_original - deviance_enhanced)
  ), 2),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
print(model_comparison_deviance)
```


**Model Selection Criteria #2: AIC and BIC (computed from the penalized log-likelihood)** 

To further compare in-sample model fit between the two nested Firth logistic regression models, we computed the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) using the models’ penalized log-likelihoods. Both criteria balance goodness of fit with a penalty for model complexity where lower values indicate a better tradeoff between fit and parsimony.

Relative to the reduced model, the enhanced model had an AIC that was lower by 26.60 units and a BIC that was lower by 18.85 units. The decreases in both criteria indicate that the improvement in fit from adding the variables, `positive_d_dimer`, `echo_rvsp_value`, and `dvt_in_lower_extremity` outweighs the penalty for including additional parameters even under BIC’s more conservative complexity penalty.

Taken together with the penalized likelihood ratio test results, these findings support selecting the enhanced model as providing better in-sample fit after accounting for its greater complexity.

```{r}
k_reduced <- length(coef(model_geneva_original_firth))   
k_full    <- length(coef(model_geneva_enhanced_firth))  

n_reduced <- model_geneva_original_firth$n
n_full    <- model_geneva_enhanced_firth$n

n <- min(n_reduced, n_full)

aic_reduced <- -2 * ll_orig + 2 * k_reduced
aic_full    <- -2 * ll_enh    + 2 * k_full

bic_reduced <- -2 * ll_orig + log(n) * k_reduced
bic_full    <- -2 * ll_enh    + log(n) * k_full

model_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Reduced (Original Geneva, Firth)",
            "Full (Enhanced Geneva, Firth)",
            "Difference (Reduced - Full)"),
  AIC = round(c(aic_reduced, aic_full, aic_reduced - aic_full), 2),
  BIC = round(c(bic_reduced, bic_full, bic_reduced - bic_full), 2),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

print(model_comparison)
```

### Comparison of Predictive Performance between 2 Models 

To evaluate and compare the predictive discrimination of the original Modified Geneva model and the enhanced model with three additional predictors, repeated stratified cross-validation was used. The analysis dataset was partitioned into 10 folds, and this procedure was repeated 5 times, yielding 50 train–test evaluations. In each evaluation, a Firth logistic regression model was fit on the training folds (9/10 of the data), predicted probabilities were generated for the held-out fold (1/10 of the data), and a test-fold AUC was computed from the ROC curve. This process was performed separately for the original and enhanced models, and the fold-wise AUC difference (enhanced − original) was calculated to quantify the incremental gain in discrimination. Finally, the mean and standard deviation of the AUC across all folds were summarized for each model and presented in a table.

**Method 1: Comparison of AUC (Area under the Curve) Values: **

Using repeated cross-validation, the out-of-sample discrimination was:

- Original Modified Geneva Model: **Average AUC = 0.8369**
- Enhanced Model: **Average AUC = 0.8570**

The mean fold-level difference in AUC across the repeated cross-validation splits was **ΔAUC = 0.0202**, indicating that the enhanced model provides a modest improvement in discrimination. The AUC measures a model’s ability to distinguish between individuals with and without pulmonary embolism across all possible classification thresholds (0.5 = no discrimination; 1.0 = perfect discrimination). Both models demonstrated strong discrimination (AUC > 0.80), with slightly higher AUC for the enhanced model.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
dat <- merged_data_no_covid[, c("pe_status", enhanced_geneva_predictors)]
dat$pe_status <- factor(dat$pe_status, levels = c("0","1"))
folds <- createMultiFolds(dat$pe_status, k = 10, times = 5)

calc_fold_auc <- function(train_idx, predictors) {
  train <- dat[train_idx, , drop = FALSE]
  test  <- dat[-train_idx, , drop = FALSE]

  fit <- logistf(pe_status ~ ., data = train[, c("pe_status", predictors)])
  p   <- predict(fit, newdata = test, type = "response")

  roc_obj <- roc(test$pe_status, p, levels = c("0","1"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
  as.numeric(auc(roc_obj))
}

auc_orig <- sapply(folds, calc_fold_auc, predictors = geneva_components)
auc_enh  <- sapply(folds, calc_fold_auc, predictors = enhanced_geneva_predictors)

cv_res <- data.frame(
  Fold = names(folds),
  AUC_Original = auc_orig,
  AUC_Enhanced = auc_enh,
  Delta_AUC = auc_enh - auc_orig
) %>%
  mutate(across(c(AUC_Original, AUC_Enhanced, Delta_AUC), ~ round(.x, 4)))

auc_summary_long <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(Metric = "AUC (Original Wells, Firth)", Mean = mean(cv_res$AUC_Original), SD = sd(cv_res$AUC_Original)),
  data.frame(Metric = "AUC (Enhanced Wells, Firth)", Mean = mean(cv_res$AUC_Enhanced), SD = sd(cv_res$AUC_Enhanced)),
  data.frame(Metric = "ΔAUC (Enhanced − Original)",  Mean = mean(cv_res$Delta_AUC),  SD = sd(cv_res$Delta_AUC))
) %>%
  mutate(across(c(Mean, SD), ~ round(.x, 4)))

auc_summary_long %>%
  kbl(
    caption = "Repeated 10-fold CV (5 repeats): Mean AUC and SD",
    col.names = c("Metric", "Mean", "SD"),
    align = "lcc",
    format = "html"
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  ) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)

tt_auc <- t.test(cv_res$AUC_Enhanced, cv_res$AUC_Original, paired = TRUE)
tt_auc
```


A paired t-test was applied to the 50 fold-level ΔAUC (enhanced-original) from the repeated 10-fold cross-validation to assess whether the enhanced model tends to yield higher AUC than the original model on the same held-out splits. The test produced **t = 3.5547, df = 49, and p = 0.0008496**, providing evidence that the ΔAUC is positive on average across the CV evaluations. Overall, these results sugget that adding `positive_d_dimer`,  `echo_rvsp_value`, and `dvt_in_lower_extremity` yields a small but consistent improvement in out of sample discrimination. 

**Method 2: Classification Performance at Optimal Cutpoint ** 

To compare the classification performance of the two firth logistic regression models, predicted probabilities were converted into binary outcomes using optimal cutpoints determined by Youden’s Index from the ROC curves. Youden’s Index, defined as (Sensitivity + Specificity – 1), identifies the threshold that maximizes the model’s ability to correctly classify positive and negative cases. Using these optimal thresholds, key performance metrics such as Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, Positive Predictive Value (PPV), and Negative Predictive Value (NPV) were calculated for both models to evaluate and compare their diagnostic performance. The Firth logistic regression models were fitted on the training folds and the training fold ROC curve was used to choose an optimal cutoff determined by Youden's index. The cutoff was then applied to the held-out fold to classify individuals as having pulmonary embolsim versus not. This process is repeated for the two models across all the folds where the averages of each metric across the 50 held out evaluations. 

**Accuracy** increased slightly from **0.7666 (original) to 0.7849 (Enhanced)** with a difference of **+0.0183**, indicating an overall increase, but negligible, in the model’s predictive ability to classify individuals correctly as having or not having pulmonary embolism.

**Sensitivity**, which measures the model’s ability to correctly identify patients with pulmonary embolism, increased from **0.6365 to 0.7141** with a difference of **+0.0776**. This suggests that the enhanced model is more sensitive meaning that it catches more true pulmonary embolism cases. **Specificity**, representing the ability to correctly identify individuals without pulmonary embolism, decreased from **0.8846 to 0.8491** with a difference of **-0.0355**, indicating that the enhanced model is marginally less effective at ruling out non-cases and may produce slightly more false positives.

In addition, **PPV** decreased slightly from **0.8472 to 0.8192** with a difference of **-0.0280**, meaning that a lower proportion of individuals predicted to have pulmonary embolism by the enhanced model were correctly classified. Conversely, **NPV** increased slightly from **0.7315 to 0.7693** with a difference of **0.0378**, suggesting a modest increase in the accuracy of identifying true negatives.

In conclusion, at Youden-optimal cutpoints, the enhanced model provides modestly higher sensitivity and NPV at the cost of a small reduction in specificity and PPV, with a slight net gain in accuracy.

```{r}
calc_metrics <- function(TP, FP, TN, FN) {
  c(
    Accuracy    = (TP + TN) / (TP + FP + TN + FN),
    Sensitivity = ifelse(TP + FN == 0, NA, TP / (TP + FN)),
    Specificity = ifelse(TN + FP == 0, NA, TN / (TN + FP)),
    PPV         = ifelse(TP + FP == 0, NA, TP / (TP + FP)),
    NPV         = ifelse(TN + FN == 0, NA, TN / (TN + FN))
  )
}

eval_fold_classification <- function(train_idx, predictors) {
  train <- dat[train_idx, , drop = FALSE]
  test  <- dat[-train_idx, , drop = FALSE]

  fit <- logistf(pe_status ~ ., data = train[, c("pe_status", predictors)])

  p_train <- predict(fit, newdata = train, type = "response")
  p_test  <- predict(fit, newdata = test,  type = "response")

  roc_train <- roc(train$pe_status, p_train, levels = c("0","1"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
  thr <- coords(roc_train, x = "best", best.method = "youden",
                ret = "threshold", transpose = FALSE)[["threshold"]]

  pred_test <- factor(ifelse(p_test >= thr, "1", "0"), levels = c("0","1"))
  y <- factor(test$pe_status, levels = c("0","1"))

  TP <- sum(pred_test == "1" & y == "1")
  FP <- sum(pred_test == "1" & y == "0")
  TN <- sum(pred_test == "0" & y == "0")
  FN <- sum(pred_test == "0" & y == "1")

  c(Threshold = thr, calc_metrics(TP, FP, TN, FN))
}

res_orig <- t(sapply(folds, eval_fold_classification, predictors = geneva_components))
res_enh  <- t(sapply(folds, eval_fold_classification, predictors = enhanced_geneva_predictors))

res_orig <- as.data.frame(res_orig); res_enh <- as.data.frame(res_enh)
res_orig$Fold  <- names(folds);      res_enh$Fold  <- names(folds)
res_orig$Model <- "Original Geneva (Firth)"
res_enh$Model  <- "Enhanced Geneva (Firth)"

cv_class <- bind_rows(res_orig, res_enh) %>%
  relocate(Model, Fold) %>%
  mutate(across(c(Threshold, Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, PPV, NPV), as.numeric))

cv_class_summary <- cv_class %>%
  group_by(Model) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean_Threshold   = mean(Threshold, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_Accuracy    = mean(Accuracy, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_Sensitivity = mean(Sensitivity, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_Specificity = mean(Specificity, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_PPV         = mean(PPV, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_NPV         = mean(NPV, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kaggle_metrics_mean <- cv_class_summary %>%
  select(Model, starts_with("Mean_")) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -Model, names_to = "Metric", values_to = "Value") %>%
  mutate(
    Metric = sub("^Mean_", "", Metric),
    Metric = case_when(
      Metric == "Threshold"   ~ "Youden Threshold",
      Metric == "Accuracy"    ~ "Accuracy",
      Metric == "Sensitivity" ~ "Sensitivity",
      Metric == "Specificity" ~ "Specificity",
      Metric == "PPV"         ~ "PPV",
      Metric == "NPV"         ~ "NPV",
      TRUE ~ Metric
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Model, values_from = Value) %>%
  rename(
    Original = `Original Geneva (Firth)`,
    Enhanced = `Enhanced Geneva (Firth)`
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Difference = Enhanced - Original,
    across(c(Original, Enhanced, Difference), ~ round(.x, 4)),
    Metric = factor(Metric, levels = c("Youden Threshold","Accuracy","Sensitivity","Specificity","PPV","NPV"))
  ) %>%
  arrange(Metric) %>%
  select(Metric, Original, Enhanced, Difference)

kaggle_metrics_mean %>%
  kbl(
    caption = "Repeated 10-fold CV (5 repeats): Mean Classification Metrics at Youden-Optimal Cutpoints",
    col.names = c("Metric", "Original Geneva (Firth)", "Enhanced Geneva (Firth)", "Difference (Enhanced − Original)"),
    align = "lccc",
    format = "html"
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  ) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
```


**Method 3: Visualization of Comparison of the ROC Curves of the Two Models **

One ROC curve was created for each model (original and enhanced). For each repeated 10-fold split, a Firth logistic regression was fit on the training data and then predicts probabilities for the testing data. These held-out predictions were then saved together with the subject's true outcome and a stable identifier (row number). Because the cross-validation was repeated 5 times, each patient was held out once per repeat and therefore received multiple out-of-fold predicted probabilities. Across 5 repeats, every patient appears in the test fold exactly once. These probabilities were then averaged for each patient to produce a single cross-validated predicted probability per patient. Using these pooled out-of-fold predictions and taking into account different thresholds, ROC curves and AUC values were computed for both models and plotted together. 

The diagonal dashed line represents the line of no discrimination (AUC = 0.5), indicating performance equivalent to random guessing. Both ROC curves lie well above this line, demonstrating that each model has meaningful discriminative ability. The enhanced model is consistently better overall as the red curve is above the blue curve for most of the false-positive rate range. This observation is supported by the increase area under the curve (AUC) for the Enhanced model (0.8554577) compared to the Original model (0.8089022), supporting the prior results earlier that there is meaningful gain in discrimination from adding the two predictors when calculating the mean AUC values. 

It is important to note that the AUC values reported earlier were mean AUCs averaged across the 50 held out folds. For the ROC plot below, AUC was instead recalculated using pooled out-of-fold predicted probabilities, where each patient’s out-of-fold predictions across repeats were averaged to yield one cross-validated probability per patient. As a result, the AUC values shown in the ROC figure may differ from the previously reported mean fold-level AUCs because they are based on a different (pooled) cross-validation summary approach.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
get_oof_preds <- function(train_idx, predictors) {
  test_idx <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(dat)), train_idx)

  train <- dat[train_idx, , drop = FALSE]
  test  <- dat[test_idx,  , drop = FALSE]

  fit <- logistf(pe_status ~ ., data = train[, c("pe_status", predictors)])
  p   <- predict(fit, newdata = test, type = "response")

  data.frame(
    row_id = test_idx,
    y      = test$pe_status,
    p      = as.numeric(p)
  )
}

oof_orig <- bind_rows(lapply(folds, get_oof_preds, predictors = geneva_components)) %>%
  group_by(row_id) %>%
  summarise(y = first(y), p = mean(p), .groups = "drop")

oof_enh <- bind_rows(lapply(folds, get_oof_preds, predictors = enhanced_geneva_predictors)) %>%
  group_by(row_id) %>%
  summarise(y = first(y), p = mean(p), .groups = "drop")

roc_original_cv <- roc(oof_orig$y, oof_orig$p, levels = c("0","1"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
roc_enhanced_cv <- roc(oof_enh$y,  oof_enh$p,  levels = c("0","1"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)

cat("Pooled AUC (Original) =", as.numeric(auc(roc_original_cv)), "\n")
cat("Pooled AUC (Enhanced) =", as.numeric(auc(roc_enhanced_cv)), "\n")

ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = 1 - roc_original_cv$specificities,
                y = roc_original_cv$sensitivities,
                color = "Original Geneva (Firth)"),
            linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = 1 - roc_enhanced_cv$specificities,
                y = roc_enhanced_cv$sensitivities,
                color = "Enhanced Geneva (Firth)"),
            linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed",
              color = "gray50", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = "1 − Specificity (False Positive Rate)",
    y = "Sensitivity (True Positive Rate)",
    title = "ROC Curve Comparison (Pooled Out-of-Fold Predictions)",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Original AUC: ", round(as.numeric(auc(roc_original_cv)), 3),
      " | Enhanced AUC: ", round(as.numeric(auc(roc_enhanced_cv)), 3)
    ),
    color = "Models"
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,1), expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1), expand = c(0,0)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### Comparison of Calibration between 2 Models 

After establishing that the addition of the three predictors improved the discriminatory ability of the enhanced Modified Geneva Score model, it is also important to assess whether the predicted probabilities align with the actual observed outcomes of pulmonary embolism. While improved discrimination indicates a model’s enhanced ability to distinguish between patients with and without PE, robust calibration ensures that the predicted probabilities accurately reflect the true likelihood of the outcome. Therefore, both discrimination and calibration must be considered when evaluating the overall predictive performance of a diagnostic model.

**Method 1: Comparison of Brier Score of Calibration ** 

The **Brier score** was computed for both the original and enhanced Firth logistic regression models to evaluate calibration or how closely the predicted probabilities of pulmonary embolism (PE) match the observed PE outcomes. Brier scores were calculated using **pooled out-of-fold predictions** from the repeated 10-fold cross-validation procedure. In each split, the Firth model was fit on the training folds and predicted probabilities were generated for the held-out fold. Because cross-validation was repeated 5 times, each patient contributed multiple out-of-fold predictions. These probabilities were then **averaged within patient** to obtain a single cross-validated predicted probability per individual. The Brier score was then computed as the mean squared error between these predicted probabilities and the observed outcomes (0/1), where lower values indicate better-calibrated and more accurate probability estimates.

The original Modified Geneva model produced a Brier score of **0.1546**, while the enhanced model achieved a lower Brier score of **0.1457**, corresponding to a **5.72% reduction**. This indicates that the enhanced model yields probability estimates that are, on average, closer to the true PE outcomes and therefore **better calibrated**. Together with the observed gains in discrimination, these results support including `positive_d_dimer`,  `echo_rvsp_value`, and `dvt_in_lower_extremity` as additions to the Modified Geneva framework to improve the model’s overall predictive performance and clinical usefulness.

```{r}
set.seed(123)

get_oof_preds <- function(train_idx, predictors) {
  test_idx <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(dat)), train_idx)

  train <- dat[train_idx, , drop = FALSE]
  test  <- dat[test_idx,  , drop = FALSE]

  fit <- logistf(pe_status ~ ., data = train[, c("pe_status", predictors)])
  p   <- predict(fit, newdata = test, type = "response")

  data.frame(
    row_id = test_idx,
    y      = test$pe_status,      
    p      = as.numeric(p)        
  )
}

oof_orig <- bind_rows(lapply(folds, get_oof_preds, predictors = geneva_components)) %>%
  group_by(row_id) %>%
  summarise(y = first(y), p = mean(p), .groups = "drop")

oof_enh <- bind_rows(lapply(folds, get_oof_preds, predictors = enhanced_geneva_predictors)) %>%
  group_by(row_id) %>%
  summarise(y = first(y), p = mean(p), .groups = "drop")

y_num_orig <- as.numeric(as.character(oof_orig$y))
y_num_enh  <- as.numeric(as.character(oof_enh$y))

brier_orig <- mean((oof_orig$p - y_num_orig)^2)
brier_enh  <- mean((oof_enh$p  - y_num_enh )^2)

cat(sprintf("Pooled OOF Brier score (Original) = %.4f\n", brier_orig))
cat(sprintf("Pooled OOF Brier score (Enhanced) = %.4f\n", brier_enh))
cat(sprintf("ΔBrier (Enhanced − Original)      = %.4f\n", brier_enh - brier_orig))

cat(sprintf("Relative Brier improvement = %.2f%%\n",
            100 * (brier_orig - brier_enh) / brier_orig))

```

**Method 2: Calibration Plot ** 

To visually compare calibration between the original and enhanced Firth logistic regression models, a calibration plot was generated using pooled out-of-fold (cross-validated) predicted probabilities. Patients were grouped into 10 equal-sized bins (deciles) based on predicted risk. Within each bin, the mean predicted probability was plotted against the observed event rate (proportion with PE). The dashed 45° line represents perfect calibration, where predicted risk equals observed risk; points above this line indicate underestimation (observed > predicted), whereas points below indicate overestimation (observed < predicted).

Upon examining the plot, the red line representing the Enhanced Geneva model closely follows the diagonal across most of the risk levels, suggesting good calibration. For example, when the model predicts roughly a 23% risk, the actual observed risk is also approximately 23%, as evidenced by the curve’s proximity to the ideal line. Across most risk ranges, the enhanced model maintains this alignment, with only a slight underestimation at higher probabilities and slight overestimation in the lower probabilities. 

In contrast, the blue line representing the Original Geneva model shows more pronounced deviations from the ideal diagnoal line. Notably, at a predicted probability of around 28%, the observed risk increases to around 63%, indicating that the model underestimates risk in this region. Conversely, at a predicted probability of about 16%, the observed risk peaks at 0%, suggesting overestimation at specific risk levels.

In summary, the calibration plot clearly demonstrates that the Enhanced Geneva model (red) provides superior calibration, as its predictions more closely align with the observed outcomes compared to the Original Geneva model (blue).

```{r}
make_calib_df <- function(oof, model_name, n_bins = 10) {
  oof %>%
    mutate(
      Model = model_name,
      y_num = as.numeric(as.character(y))
    ) %>%
    mutate(bin = ntile(p, n_bins)) %>%
    group_by(Model, bin) %>%
    summarise(
      mean_pred = mean(p, na.rm = TRUE),
      obs_rate  = mean(y_num, na.rm = TRUE),
      n         = n(),
      .groups   = "drop"
    )
}

calib_orig <- make_calib_df(oof_orig, "Original Geneva (Firth)", n_bins = 10)
calib_enh  <- make_calib_df(oof_enh,  "Enhanced Geneva (Firth)", n_bins = 10)

calib_df <- bind_rows(calib_orig, calib_enh)

ggplot(calib_df, aes(x = mean_pred, y = obs_rate, group = Model, color = Model)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Calibration Plot (Pooled Out-of-Fold Predictions)",
    x = "Mean predicted probability (within bin)",
    y = "Observed event rate (within bin)",
    color = "Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```
